steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Film scene analysis requires systematic examination of how micro features including cinematography, mise-en-scene, editing and sound create meaning and generate response.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Begin by watching the extract at least twice: first for overall impression and narrative content, then for detailed identification of specific film language techniques.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Cinematography analysis covers shot type, camera angle, camera movement, composition, focus and lighting, each of which contributes to meaning and audience positioning.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Mise-en-scene analysis examines setting, props, costume, performance, hairstyle and makeup, considering how each element has been deliberately chosen to communicate meaning.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always watch the extract at least twice before writing, using the first viewing for overall impression and the second for detailed notes. Use precise film language terminology: say 'extreme close-up' not 'really close shot' and 'non-diegetic orchestral score' not 'background music'. Organise your analysis around key moments or significant techniques rather than working through the extract shot by shot. Every point you make must connect a technique to an effect on meaning or audience response, not just describe what you see. Build towards an overall interpretation of the sequence rather than leaving your analysis as disconnected observations.
